claims.text: Reporting period and statutory basis: 'The Department of War (DoW) provides this report pursuant to a requirement established under section 3373k of Title 50, United States Code. This document contains all reported unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP)-related events occurring from June 2, 2024, to May 30, 2025, and UAP-related events occurring within any previous period not covered in a previous report.'

claims.nodeLabel: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
claims.text: Section G, 'Capture or Exploitation of UAP' (p. 9), in full: 'To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG. AARO's development process draws on established USG capabilities and operating procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel.' This is AARO's most recent on-the-record denial of any recovery/exploitation program, paired with an admission that no handling process yet exists.

claims.nodeLabel: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
claims.text: Acknowledged collection bias: 'a collection bias favoring the continental United States, its littoral waters, and global U.S. military operational areas, influences AARO's UAP case holdings. Locations with a higher density of U.S. military sensors and assets tend to submit more UAP reports.' And: 'A lack of timely and actionable sensor data continues to constrain AARO's ability to resolve cases.'

claims.nodeLabel: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
claims.text: INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY on satellite-flaring resolutions. The Executive Summary (p. 2) states: 'During the reporting period, AARO onboarded a new capability that enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring.' Section C, 'Notable Trends Regarding Prosaic Objects' (p. 8), states: 'AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period.' The two figures - 238 and 44 - are not reconciled anywhere in the document.

claims.nodeLabel: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
claims.text: Section H (p. 9): 'To date, AARO has not received a UAP report in which a reporter described sustaining adverse health effects associated with their experience. However, AARO will document any UAP-related health effects, should they be reported.'

claims.nodeLabel: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
claims.text: The report contradicts itself on satellite flaring. Section IV.C states that AARO resolved 44 UAP-related events as attributable to satellite flaring during the reporting period, while Section I (Executive Summary) and Section VI state that new capability enabled analysts to resolve 238 reported UAP as satellite flaring. Note that a separate figure of 44 UAP reports 'in the space domain' appears at Section III.A and is a different 44.

claims.nodeLabel: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
claims.text: Section F (p. 9): 'AARO received 50 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding unmanned aerial systems (UAS) incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons, and launch sites, a 177.8 percent increase over the 18 reported in AARO's FY 2024 annual report. None of these incidents were reported as UAP.' Of the 50, '33 of 50 (66 percent) ... involved one UAS, with the other 17 involving between 2 and 7 UAS. Most cases - 47 of the 50 - occurred between 1700 and 0500 local time.' Five persisted at least an hour, 'with the longest recorded at approximately three hours.'

claims.text: Caseload: 'The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) received 319 reports of UAP-related events. Of those, 284 feature UAP-related events occurring during the reporting period.' This is a sharp drop from the 757 reports of FY2024.

claims.nodeLabel: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
claims.text: The FY2025 report was delivered roughly 14 months after its own information cut-off (30 May 2025 cut-off, PDF generated 10 June 2026, posted 20 July 2026) - the longest lag of any AARO annual report to date. Reasoning: comparison of stated cut-off dates against PDF creation dates and index posting dates across FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025.

claims.nodeLabel: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
claims.text: The 238 vs 44 satellite-flaring discrepancy matters because 238 exceeds the 284 in-period reports the FY2025 report says AARO received; if 238 in-period cases were resolved as satellite flaring the residual unexplained set would be near-negligible, whereas the Section C figure of 44 leaves a far larger residual. The report's headline resolution rate cannot be reconstructed from its own published numbers. Reasoning: arithmetic comparison of the Executive Summary, Section III caseload and Section C figures within a single document.

By the FY2025 reporting cycle AARO is a Department of War component, not a Department of Defense component: the FY2025 report's cover reads 'DEPARTMENT OF WAR / ALL-DOMAIN ANOMALY RESOLUTION OFFICE', where the FY2024 report cover read 'THE DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE / ALL-DOMAIN ANOMALY RESOLUTION OFFICE'. The DoD IG's own site likewise now brands as the Department of War Office of Inspector General.

AARO's statutory annual reporting requirement is codified at 50 U.S.C. Sec. 3373k. The FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report states: 'The Department of War (DoW) provides this report pursuant to a requirement established under section 3373k of Title 50, United States Code.'

edges.label: COMPARISON: AARO's Foreign Partner Engagement section names no Latin American partner at all
edges.note: COMPARISON EDGE, and a sourced negative. Section V.A of AARO's FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report is two sentences in full: 'During the reporting period, AARO continued to engage with international partners to exchange information and best practices for UAP reporting, analysis, and response. AARO's deputy director presented a mission briefing to the Defense Geospatial Intelligence conference in London, United Kingdom.' No foreign office, no foreign air force and no foreign archive is named anywhere in the document except that one London conference. Brazil, the FAB and the Arquivo Nacional — the largest declassified military UAP holding in the Americas — do not appear. The task asked what the section actually names: it names one conference in London and nothing else.
